clue.text: Two teams divided or together?

parts.note: a team is a side, and there are two of them here
in arithmetic one number is divided by another, so the word supplies the little word between the sides

explanation.surface: A question about whether two teams are split apart or united.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two teams' gives one side at each end, with 'divided' lending the 'by' of 'divided by' between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Things placed next to each other, or working jointly, are together in both senses of the phrase.

clue.text: Discharge rifle

definitions.meaning: to dismiss someone from a job
to plunder or ransack, as a looting army might

explanation.surface: An instruction to fire a gun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rifle' looks like a gun, but here it is the verb meaning to loot.
explanation.definitionFit: To dismiss an employee is to fire them, and to pillage a town is an old sense of plundering it; one word covers both.

clue.text: Speech in the novel beginning differently

indicators.note: the opening letter of the word for novels is swapped for another one

explanation.surface: A description of how a character talks in a book that opens in an unusual way.
explanation.definitionFit: Diction is a person's manner of speaking or enunciation, so it stands for speech.

clue.text: Put the spotlight on British rowing — invite changes

indicators.note: the letters of the two words that follow are changed around into a new order

explanation.surface: A sports news line: British rowing is in the limelight after an invitation shakes things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British rowing' reads as a sport in the news, but only the B of British stays put; 'changes' scrambles the other two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To make something visible or prominent is to highlight it, the idiom meaning to spotlight it.

clue.text: A lot must, surprisingly revealing all?

indicators.note: the letters of the three words before turn up in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: A puzzled remark that a great deal must, unexpectedly, be disclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: The full amount added up is the whole of something, everything there is.

clue.text: Shoots game

definitions.meaning: the pub sport of throwing small arrows at a board

explanation.surface: A headline about firing at quarry.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick sudden movement is a dart, and the pub sport played with small arrows at a board is called by the plural.

clue.text: Primate playing host to southern sector of Church

indicators.note: a host takes a guest in, so the primate's word holds the abbreviation inside it

explanation.surface: A monkey entertaining guests in the southern part of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' suggests a bishop or archbishop in a church setting, but here it is an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: The apse is the semicircular recess at the east end of a church, one part of the building.

clue.text: Left one on allotment

parts.note: port is the left side of a ship
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone left alone on their vegetable plot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'allotment' suggests a British garden plot rented from the council, but it is used in its sense of a share.
explanation.definitionFit: An allotment is an amount allotted, a share or helping, which is what a portion is.

clue.text: Simple way to achieve financial security

parts.note: a street is a way, a road

explanation.surface: Advice on an uncomplicated route to being comfortably off.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on this idiomatic road means living in comfort without money worries.

clue.text: Plants from cold climates initially bedded in at one

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: the initial is set down inside the little word like a plant in a bed
the first letter of the word it follows is taken

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gardener's note about plants from chilly regions being planted at one spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes the C of 'climates', and 'bedded in' puts it inside AT, between C for cold and I for one.
explanation.definitionFit: Cacti are spiny desert succulents, a kind of plant.

clue.text: Male hanging round mine for festival

indicators.note: the hanging goes round the other piece, enclosing it

parts.note: an arras is a tapestry hung on a wall
a dig is an excavation, a mine

explanation.surface: A man loitering around a colliery, waiting for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hanging' looks like a verb about the man loitering, but it is a noun: a wall tapestry.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrove Tuesday's carnival, famous in New Orleans, is a festival before Lent.

clue.text: Woman and husband with historical object being shown round bar in country, unofficially

indicators.note: the historical object goes round the bar like a guide showing someone round

parts.note: a relic is an object surviving from the past

explanation.surface: A couple carrying an antique are given a tour of a bar somewhere abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unofficially' is part of the definition: the state's formal name is Ireland or Éire.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal name for the state of Ireland, as distinct from Northern Ireland, which remains in the UK.

clue.text: Cheerful kind, wearing trendy shades

indicators.note: the outer pieces have the other on them, wrapping it

explanation.surface: A kind-hearted person in fashionable sunglasses, looking happy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a happy, upbeat mood is the idiom's meaning, so it fits a cheerful person.

clue.text: GP, too, seeks out village near Slough

indicators.note: the letters of the words before are put out of their usual order

explanation.surface: A family doctor, too, goes looking for a village near Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: Stoke Poges is a Buckinghamshire village west of London, known for Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard'; Slough is a nearby English town.
explanation.definitionFit: The place is a small village a few miles north of the town of Slough in southern England.

clue.text: Carpentry tool one wants, badly

indicators.note: the letters of the two words before are arranged badly, out of order

explanation.surface: Someone wants a woodworking tool very much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' reads as 'very much' with 'wants' but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A fine-toothed saw used for cutting joints in woodwork, a carpenter's tool.

clue.text: Star's black eye?

definitions.meaning: something that shines brightly in the sky
a bruised eye after a punch, in slang

explanation.surface: A question whether a celebrity has a bruised eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that gives off light, such as a star, can be called this, and it is also slang for a bruised eye.

clue.text: Unnerved seeing old girl take the plunge

parts.note: to take the plunge is an idiom for getting married

explanation.surface: Someone is nervous seeing an elderly woman decide to marry, or to dive.
explanation.definitionFit: To be daunted or intimidated by something impressive leaves one unnerved.

clue.text: King careless concerning warning device

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for king in chess

explanation.surface: A monarch is negligent about an alarm.
explanation.definitionFit: A loud electric horn, once fitted to cars and ships, is used to sound an alarm.

clue.text: Unscrupulous type in area instructed sailor to come over

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming over means turning over, so the two pieces read upwards

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: A shady character in the district told a seaman to come across.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'to come over' turns the two pieces upwards; 'in' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes a dishonest or disreputable person, a rogue.

clue.text: Compete in a further sports centre in Scotland

indicators.note: the word for compete sits inside the other pieces

explanation.surface: An invitation to compete in another sporting venue in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Aviemore is a resort in the Scottish Highlands, a centre for skiing and outdoor sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cairngorms town is a base for skiing and outdoor activities, so a Scottish sports centre.

clue.text: Daughter coming in to mend broken bit

indicators.note: the single letter enters the reshuffled letters
the letters of the two words before are broken up and reshuffled

explanation.surface: A daughter arrives to repair a broken piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' turns TO MEND into ODMENT; 'coming in' puts D inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: An odd leftover piece or scrap is a bit.

clue.text: Having amorous affairs is what 24's hubby enjoys?

definitions.meaning: 24 across is the wife neglected for golf, so her husband enjoys a game on the course

explanation.surface: Infidelity is what the husband of the woman at 24 likes.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the second word: playing a round of golf.
explanation.definitionFit: Being unfaithful or flirting with others is a colloquial sense, and a golfer plays a round.

clue.text: Dizzy, theologian being held by foreign soldier close to sacristy

indicators.note: the theologian is held inside the other letters

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier, foreign to a British setter

indicators.note: the close, or last letter, of the word that follows is taken

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a theologian

explanation.surface: A theologian is light-headed, gripped by an overseas soldier near the sacristy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' looks like 'near' but takes the last letter of 'sacristy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Giddy means having a whirling sensation, the same as being dizzy.

clue.text: The woman duke got rid of

explanation.surface: The woman the duke discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: To shed something is to cast it off, as a tree loses leaves, so to discard it.

clue.text: Her man on a course? Most of the time, it seems!

definitions.text: Her man on a course? Most of the time, it seems!

parts.words: Her man on a course? Most of the time, it seems!
parts.note: describes a wife whose husband spends so long on the links that she might as well be bereaved

explanation.surface: A wife complains that her husband is on a course nearly all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'course' suggests study, but it is the golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A humorous term for a woman left alone because her husband is always out playing on the links.

clue.text: Freeloader given shelter by church

parts.note: lee is shelter from the wind

explanation.surface: A sponger taken in by a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A leech is a person who lives off others, a parasite or sponger.

clue.text: Starts to see inconsistencies throughout elaborate plot

indicators.note: the opening letters of the four following words are taken

explanation.surface: Someone begins to notice contradictions all through a complicated storyline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plot' looks like a story but means a piece of land.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot of ground for building on is a site.

clue.text: Many a cartoon strip is so extremely silly — shown one I overlooked

definitions.text: Many a cartoon strip is so

indicators.note: the extremes, first and last letters, of the next word are taken
the single letter is overlooked, left out of the word for shown

explanation.surface: A comic strip that is exceedingly foolish, and a reader admits to missing it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' gives SY from 'silly'; 'overlooked' drops one I from INDICATED, leaving NDICATED.
explanation.definitionFit: Cartoon strips are often sold to many newspapers at once through an agency, which describes them this way.
